prompt: What can a web application firewall see that a network firewall cannot?

choices.text: The client's IP address and port number
choices.why: A network firewall sees those too.

choices.text: The request itself
choices.why: Right. Path, headers and body.

choices.text: The database's queries, as they run
choices.why: It sees HTTP, not what the application does with it.

choices.text: Traffic between two virtual machines in the same subnet
choices.why: It sits in front of HTTP endpoints, not between VMs.

prompt: Match each situation to where the WAF belongs.

pairs.left: Stop attacks before they reach the region
Protect backends that have only private addresses
Serve customers worldwide with caching at the edge

prompt: A scan finds SQL injection in the search endpoint, and the WAF blocks the pattern. What is still to do?
hint: A guard at a door with a broken lock.

choices.text: Nothing; the managed rule set covers SQL injection
choices.why: Patterns can be evaded; the code is still vulnerable.

choices.text: Switch the policy to Detection so the logs show it
choices.why: That would stop blocking a known attack.

choices.text: Fix the query itself, in the search endpoint's code
choices.why: Right. The WAF buys time; parameterised queries are the fix.

choices.text: Add a geo rule that blocks traffic from outside Brazil
choices.why: Attackers rent addresses anywhere; the code stays broken.

prompt: In which order does the shop's Front Door policy evaluate its rules?

choices.text: checkoutRateLimit, onlyBrazilForAdmin, then the managed sets
choices.why: Right. Custom rules first, lowest priority number first.

choices.text: The managed sets, then the custom rules
choices.why: Custom rules come first.

choices.text: onlyBrazilForAdmin, then checkoutRateLimit
choices.why: Priority 10 comes before 20.

choices.text: All rules at once, in parallel
choices.why: They are evaluated in order, and the first decisive match acts.

prompt: How many requests to /checkout per minute from one client does checkoutRateLimit allow before blocking?
Why is onlyBrazilForAdmin not what protects the administration path?

choices.text: Geo rules are only evaluated in Detection mode
choices.why: They work in both modes.

choices.text: negateCondition makes it allow everything
choices.why: It turns the match into not-Brazil, as intended.

choices.text: Front Door cannot read the request path
choices.why: It can; the rule matches on RequestUri.

choices.text: Brazilian addresses are for rent too
choices.why: Right. It cuts scanner noise; the sign-in with a second factor protects the path.

prompt: A new WAF policy starts in the mode called ___, which logs matches and blocks nothing.
What question does the shop ask of the WAF's logs before switching to Prevention?

choices.text: How many attacks were blocked last month
choices.why: In Detection nothing was blocked; and blocks mostly count scanners.

choices.text: Which rules matched legitimate requests
choices.why: Right. Each is a false positive to remove first.

choices.text: Which country sent the most traffic
choices.why: That says nothing about whether blocking would hurt customers.

choices.text: Whether the managed rule set is the latest
choices.why: Version is a separate decision.

prompt: The default rule set keeps matching customers' searches. Which fix does the lesson recommend?
hint: Narrow holes are better than wide ones.

choices.text: Turn the matching rule off for the whole site
choices.why: That removes protection everywhere to fix one field.

choices.text: Leave the policy in Detection permanently
choices.why: Then it is a log, not a firewall.

choices.text: Remove the search box
choices.why: The shop needs search; the WAF should fit the shop.

choices.text: An exclusion for the `search` argument, with its reason written down
choices.why: Right. One argument, one rule set, documented.

prompt: Put the shop's path from a new policy to blocking in order.
items: Read which rules matched legitimate requests
Add narrow exclusions for the false positives
Switch the mode to Prevention through the pipeline
trap: Switching before reading the logs is the slip: the false positives are found by customers instead.

prompt: Why is the number of blocked requests a poor measure of a WAF's value?
hint: Who sends most of what is blocked?

choices.text: It mostly counts scanners hitting the site
choices.why: Right. False positives, custom-rule hits and rules still in Detection say more.

choices.text: Blocked requests are not logged
choices.why: They are logged; that is how they are counted.

choices.text: Blocks are billed and inspections are not
choices.why: Inspection is what is billed.

choices.text: A higher number always means a worse policy
choices.why: It means nothing either way, which is the point.

prompt: Which of these did this lesson do? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Compile a Front Door WAF policy with two custom rules
choices.why: Yes. bicep build.

choices.text: Compile a regional policy with an exclusion
choices.why: Yes. appgw-waf.bicep.

choices.text: Block a request in Prevention mode
choices.why: No. No WAF was deployed.

choices.text: Read a week of WAF logs for false positives
choices.why: No. A WAF log needs a WAF.
